title: RAG that doesn't lie: answer from the source (or don't)
desc:
Ship an LLM on your own docs and it will answer confidently — and make things up. RAG fixes that: retrieve the real page, answer from it, cite it, and refuse when the answer isn't there. Then verify it's grounded with a faithfulness check you can gate a deploy on.

You'll learn:
• Why a bigger model doesn't fix hallucination (it's honesty, not smarts)
• Retrieval: chunk → embed → nearest-neighbor search (top-k)
• Answering from context + citations
• The one-line guardrail that makes it say 'I don't know'
• Faithfulness evals — a number, not a vibe

Build this exact system, free, in your browser → https://sageideas.dev/academy

Proof, not paper.

title: LLM Evals: stop shipping on vibes — test your AI for real
desc:
'It works in the three examples I tried' is not a test — it's a vibe. This is how you actually measure an LLM feature: a dataset of real cases, a metric that scores them, and a gate that blocks regressions before they ship.

You'll learn:
• Ground-truth datasets (your answer key)
• Metrics: exact match, semantic, and LLM-as-judge with a rubric
• Wiring the score into CI so bad changes can't deploy
• Slicing the score so a healthy average can't hide a broken category
• Growing a golden set from production failures

Build the eval harness, free → https://sageideas.dev/academy

Proof, not paper.

title: Embeddings & vector search: why "nearest" isn't "relevant"
desc:
Search that matches meaning, not keywords — that's embeddings. But the closest vector isn't always the right passage, and that gap quietly wrecks RAG demos. Here's the full pipeline done right.

You'll learn:
• Embeddings: turning text into meaning-vectors
• Cosine similarity and nearest-neighbor search
• Why nearest ≠ most relevant — and how re-ranking fixes it
• Hybrid search: vectors for meaning + keywords for precision

title: Chunking: the boring choice that makes or breaks RAG
desc:
Same docs, same model, garbage answers — nine times out of ten it's how you chopped up the docs. Chunking is a knob, not a guess. Here's how to split so retrieval actually works.

You'll learn:
• Why chunks that are too big dilute and too small lose context
• Splitting on structure (paragraphs/headings), not character count
• Overlap so ideas across the seam aren't lost
• Tagging source for citations
• Treating chunking as a knob you eval
